monitored_text: Brittleness November 24, 2026 What Is Brittleness? Brittle vs. Ductile Materials Explained By Protolabs A shattered 3D print or a cracked CNC component often traces back to putting a brittle material under a dynamic load. Unlike ductile materials, which bend and yield, brittle ones offer high stiffness but can more easily snap. Knowing how to balance strength, stiffness, and toughness keeps functional parts from failing when put to work. What Is Brittleness? Brittleness is a material’s tendency to fracture under stress with little or no plastic deformation. Instead of yielding and stretching before failure, a brittle material goes almost directly from elastic deformation to fracture. Metals yield because dislocations can move through their crystal structure. In ceramics, rigid ionic and covalent bonds restrict that movement. Glass, meanwhile, has no crystal structure at all; once a crack forms, nothing blunts its tip, so it spreads rapidly. Brittleness isn't the same as weakness. Technical ceramics, for example, are brittle but have very high compressive strength and hardness. While they can be strong, brittle materials lack toughness, which is the ability to absorb energy before fracturing. A brittle material can score highly on strength and stiffness, yet score poorly on toughness. Read more about stiffness vs. strength . Brittle vs. Ductile Materials: What's the Difference? Ductility is the opposite of brittleness. It’s the material's ability to deform plastically before it fractures. When placed under increasing stress, a ductile material deforms elastically, yields, then stretches and "necks" (narrows at one point) before breaking. Ductile parts usually bend or stretch noticeably before they fail, whereas brittle parts often fail suddenly and completely. Property Brittle Materials Ductile Materials Plastic deformation before fracture Little to none Significant Fracture behavior Sudden, with flat, clean fracture surfaces Gradual, with necking and rough, fibrous surfaces Elongation at break Below 5% for metals; often under 1% for ceramics and glass Above 5% for metals; many polymers exceed 200% Impact resistance Low High Examples Glass, ceramics, gray cast iron, acrylic Aluminum, copper, mild steel, polypropylene On a stress-strain curve, a brittle material's line climbs steeply and stops. A ductile material's line bends over at the yield point and continues across a long plastic region. The larger area under that curve makes ductile materials tougher. Examples of Brittle and Ductile Materials Many common manufacturing materials exhibit brittleness or ductility. Brittle materials include: Ceramics such as alumina and zirconia, which are hard and wear-resistant, but impact-sensitive. Glass: almost no plastic deformation at room temperature. Gray cast iron: graphite flakes in its microstructure act as internal crack starters. Certain plastics such as PLA, general-purpose polystyrene, and acrylic (PMMA), which tend to crack or craze under load. Ductile materials include: Aluminum: easy to machine and form, and stays ductile at low temperatures. Copper: ductile enough to be drawn into wire. Low-carbon steel: elongates significantly before failure. Certain polymers such as polypropylene and polyethylene, which flex repeatedly without cracking, and polycarbonate, which absorbs impact well. Comparison of Ductility and Brittleness in Materials Material Behavior Elongation at Break Common Uses Stainless Steel 304 Ductile 40–60% Food-grade, medical, and corrosion-resistant parts Gray cast iron Brittle 0–2% Machine bases, engine blocks, brake rotors Polycarbonate Ductile 80–120% Impact-resistant covers, lenses, enclosures Polypropylene Highly ductile 200–600% Living hinges, containers, snap-fit closures Acrylic (PMMA) Brittle 2–5% Light pipes, displays, clear covers PLA Relatively brittle 6–10% Prototypes and visual models Values vary by grade, so refer to material data sheets before deciding to use it. For side-by-side specs, see our material comparison guide . What Causes Brittleness in Materials? Just how brittle a material is or becomes hinges on several factors. You’ll need to pay attention to them if you decide to use a brittle material. Temperature Many materials become more brittle as they get colder. For example, carbon steels have a ductile-to-brittle transition temperature below which they lose most of their toughness, while aluminum and copper don't show such a sharp transition. Polymers also lose toughness in the cold, whereas polypropylene becomes noticeably more brittle near freezing temperature. Composition and Microstructure Higher carbon content makes steel harder but less ductile, while finer grains generally improve toughness. In polymers, glass or carbon fiber fillers increase stiffness and strength, but can reduce elongation and impact resistance. Processing, Heat Treatment, and Environment Quenching hardenable steels produces hard but brittle martensite, which is why they're tempered afterward. Cold working reduces ductility, while annealing can restore it. Over time, hydrogen embrittlement, UV degradation, and chemical stress cracking can all make materials more brittle. How Is Brittleness Measured? A material’s exact brittleness is determined by putting it to the test, whether it’s tensile strength, ability to withstand impact, or how much it can stretch before breaking. Tensile Testing and Elongation at Break A tensile test pulls a sample until it breaks. Elongation at break (how much a material stretches before it breaks) is the most direct indicator of ductility. Low elongation means brittle behavior. Impact Testing and Fracture Toughness Charpy and Izod tests measure the energy a notched sample absorbs when struck by a pendulum. Fracture toughness (K IC ) measures how well a material resists the growth of an existing crack. Understanding Material Data Sheets Compare elongation at break, notched impact strength, and test temperature together. A plastic that performs well at room temperature may behave very differently at -4°F (-20°C). How Does Brittleness Affect Manufacturing and Part Design? By understanding brittleness, designers and engineers choose the right material for the right manufacturing process. CNC Machining In CNC machining , brittle materials like acrylic and ceramics can chip or crack from cutting forces or clamping pressure. In these cases, engineers require sharp tools, lighter cuts, and careful fixturing to create parts. Injection Molding Parts like snap-fits or clips, or those with thin walls flex during assembly and use, which means brittle plastics often crack when used for such applications. Molded-in stresses, weld lines, and sharp internal corners can also make a tough resin behave in a brittle way. If you are injection-molding parts with these features, consider using tougher resins such as polypropylene or polycarbonate, which can provide the ductility necessary to flex without cracking. 3D Printing PLA and many standard photopolymer resins are relatively brittle, while nylon and TPU offer more impact resistance. You should also consider print orientation, especially in fused deposition modeling (FDM) , where layer bonds are weaker than the material within each layer. Powder-bed processes like selective laser sintering (SLS) and Multi Jet Fusion (MJF) can produce more uniform properties. Design Considerations Sharp corners, holes, and notches concentrate stress, which brittle materials can't yield to relieve. When manufacturing with a brittle material, add generous fillets and avoid sudden wall thickness changes. You should also consider the load type; brittle materials handle compression well, but perform poorly under tension, bending, and impact. How to Choose Between Brittle and Ductile Materials Brittle materials are often harder, stiffer, and more wear-resistant than ductile ones. They work best where loads are mostly compressive and impacts are unlikely. Examples here include ceramics in cutting tools and wear-resistant liners, as well as concrete in columns and foundations (which are under compressive loads). Ductility is important when parts face impact, vibration, or cyclic loading, or where sudden failure creates a safety risk. Structural steel in beams that must deform without suddenly breaking is ductile, as is copper in wires that need to bend without snapping. In most applications, the right choice balances strength, stiffness, and toughness rather than maximizing one over the other. Compare elongation and impact data alongside strength and modulus, then match the material to the part's real loads and temperatures. Frequently Asked Questions Is brittleness the same as hardness? expand_less expand_more No. Hardness is resistance to indentation or scratching. Many hard materials are brittle, but a material can be hard without being especially brittle. Can a brittle material be strong? expand_less expand_more Yes. Ceramics, for instance, have very high compressive strength. Brittleness describes how a material fails, not how much load it can carry. Why do plastic parts become brittle over time? expand_less expand_more UV exposure breaks down polymer chains, and chemical contact under stress can cause environmental stress cracking. Can heat treatment reduce brittleness? expand_less expand_more Often, yes. Annealing and tempering can restore ductility in metals, although usually at the cost of some hardness or strength.
